turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Good morning, Mrs Hale. If you'd slip your coat off that arm, I'll check your blood pressure before the doctor sees you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course. I am grateful you could fit me in.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): One hundred and thirty-six over eighty-two, pulse seventy-six. That's on the screen for Doctor Rahman, and he'll call you in a moment.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, Mrs Hale, do come and sit down. How have you been keeping?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Very well, thank you, Doctor. I mustn't complain.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): This is your routine review for the blood pressure and the cholesterol. How have the tablets been going?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I feel I ought to be plain with you. I have stopped the cholesterol tablet.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thank you for telling me. Was that the atorvastatin?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, the atorvastatin, twenty milligrams. I read an article online about muscle damage, and I thought it prudent to stop.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did you take the last one?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): It was a health website, rather alarming, and my neighbour forwarded it. It spoke of aches, and of trouble with the liver.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): I can see why that unsettled you. Even roughly, when was the last dose?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I couldn't give you a proper date. Sometime after Easter, perhaps six weeks ago, but I am really not certain.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's all right. Did you actually get any muscle pain, or was it only the article?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No muscle pain at all. I felt perfectly well while I was taking it. I simply took fright.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the ramipril, for the blood pressure — are you still taking that?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, five milligrams. I must confess, though, that I take it only every other day, not every morning as the label says.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): What made you space it out?

[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): I worried a daily dose might be too strong. My husband takes metformin for his diabetes, and those seem so powerful that I thought less of mine would be safer. We keep the boxes in the same cupboard.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): His metformin is his, and his diabetes sits with his own nurse, not with you. Your ramipril is meant for every day. There'll be no scolding.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): You are very kind. I do apologise for the muddle.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Please don't. Any headaches recently, or any swelling at the ankles?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches, and my ankles are quite as usual.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about light-headedness when you stand up?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose, sometimes, not really.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll leave that as unclear. Any chest pain, or shortness of breath on the stairs?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Harold has been on those diabetes tablets for years. His nurse says his sugar is much better, though he skips them at the weekend.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): He can raise that at his own visit. For you, though — any chest pain, or getting puffed?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing of that sort. I manage the stairs without any difficulty.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): And how is your sleep?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I sleep very soundly, thank you.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): The raised blood pressure and the high cholesterol have been with you a long while, yes?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. The blood pressure for years, and the high cholesterol was found at the same time. Both are still ongoing, so I understand.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): They are — both still on your record. Have you ever smoked?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I never have, I'm glad to say.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): And are you out and about in the day?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): I live with Harold in the bungalow, and I walk to the shops most mornings.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's a nice pattern. Let me listen to your chest and look at the ankles.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): The chest is clear, the heart sounds are normal, and there's no swelling at the ankles.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): You look a little windswept. Did the weather spoil the weekend?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): It did rather. Our grandson Thomas had his school cricket match cancelled on Saturday. The covers blew off and the rain came in sideways.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Was it a proper fixture or just a friendly?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Only a friendly, against the school across the river. He was terribly proud of his new whites. We sat in the car with a flask and watched the covers flapping.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): A very British afternoon. Did he mind awfully?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): He was philosophical, as eight-year-olds can be. He insists the local side never wins when he brings the orange squash, so he felt the rain had spared them.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Superstition starts young. Is there a rematch?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Next weekend, if the sun they promised actually appears. I shall be on the boundary with a blanket, whatever the forecast says.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): I hope the squash theory holds. Now, back to the tablets, if I may.

[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): On today's reading the pressure looks acceptable, though I'm less sure it's truly controlled on alternate-day ramipril. I won't restart a statin today. I'll arrange blood tests for your cholesterol, your kidney function and your liver, and we'll revisit the statin decision in a month.

[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the cholesterol has climbed sharply, we might try a low dose of a different statin, but only if the numbers justify it. And if those vague moments turn into proper dizzy spells, we might do a heart tracing then — not today, and not on a maybe.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. I shall try to be more sensible about what I read.

[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Please take the ramipril every day, five milligrams each morning, and telephone the surgery if you feel truly unwell on it. Leave Harold's metformin entirely to Harold. Reception will book the bloods and the review in a month.
[SEG0053] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Mrs Hale, I've booked your bloods for Thursday morning and the review with Doctor Rahman in a month. The form is here whenever you're ready.

spec.situation: Patient on routine review who admits stopping the cholesterol tablet after reading something online, still takes the BP tablet but 'every other day'; mentions husband's diabetes pills; doctor does not scold, plans repeat blood tests and revisits the statin decision in a month.
features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

bad.reason: Ongoing high cholesterol supported, but patient says it was found with blood pressure, not explicitly 'for years'.

omissions.text: Patient said she stopped atorvastatin because an online article/neighbour-forwarded health website about muscle damage and liver trouble frightened her, despite feeling well on it.
While taking atorvastatin, she had no symptoms and felt perfectly well; the stop was not due to side effects.
Ramipril 5 mg was intended to be taken every morning/daily, and the doctor explicitly advised resuming daily morning dosing rather than alternate-day use.
Reason for taking ramipril only every other day: patient worried a daily dose might be too strong, influenced by confusion with her husband's metformin kept in the same cupboard.
Light-headedness on standing was asked about and the response was equivocal/unclear ('sometimes, not really'); doctor documented this as unclear.
Doctor said not to restart any statin today pending blood results.
If cholesterol has climbed sharply, doctor may try a low dose of a different statin, not atorvastatin specifically.
Blood tests were actually booked for Thursday morning.
